strengths: Addresses an important efficiency problem with a simple approach that reuses CLIP attention and key features to reduce visual tokens before the LLM. The design could complement weight quantization without requiring a separate learned compressor.

The reported reduction from 576 to approximately 40 visual tokens is substantial. Evaluation covers six benchmarks and both 7B and 13B LLaVA variants, with fine-tuned models retaining POPE performance and largely preserving ScienceQA performance.

The ablations provide useful evidence for merging and fine-tuning. Adding token supplementation improves MME from 1221.6 to 1350.3 in Table 4; fine-tuning improves POPE from 76.2 to 86.3 in Table 5. Training-free results also substantially outperform grid sampling on TextVQA.

The high-level pipeline and diagrams are understandable. Core models, datasets, and relevant pruning and merging work are cited, and Section 6 appropriately acknowledges lossy compression and restricted validation.
weaknesses: The comparisons do not adequately establish the contribution beyond existing token-reduction ideas. Table 3 considers only first-N and grid sampling, omitting fixed top-k CLS-attention selection, pooling, and established pruning or merging methods under matched token budgets and training. In particular, the benefit of IQR-based adaptivity over ordinary attention-based selection remains unisolated.

The repeated claims of comparable performance and preserved reasoning understate meaningful losses. In Table 1, the fine-tuned 7B model drops from 78.5 to 72.0 on VQAv2 and from 1510.7 to 1350.3 on MME. Without fine-tuning, POPE falls from 85.9 to 76.2. These could be worthwhile compression tradeoffs, but accuracy-versus-token-budget curves are needed to characterize them convincingly.

The central efficiency evidence consists of roofline estimates for LLM prefill with an assumed 40-token text prompt. Table 2 provides no measured end-to-end latency or memory, and does not establish the effects of pruning/merging overhead, decoding, or batching variable token counts. Its reported FLOPs also change with quantization precision without explaining the counting convention. Practical acceleration therefore remains insufficiently demonstrated.

Important implementation details are unresolved. Algorithm 1 does not specify the neighbor count k or attention-head aggregation. Its update sums neighboring tokens without explicit normalization or inclusion of the retained center, whereas Figure 2 describes weighted averaging. Cluster overlap and the distinction between dot-product and cosine similarity are also unclear. Missing LoRA and optimization settings further hinder reproduction; these ambiguities affect the implemented method, not merely presentation.

The adaptive-allocation argument relies mainly on a few visualizations. There are no retained-token-count distributions, threshold-sensitivity results, or quantitative tests connecting allocation to image complexity or task difficulty. Evaluation is also confined to LLaVA-1.5 with the same CLIP encoder at 336-pixel resolution, leaving broader applicability unestablished.
